slides.text: As the chief restaurant critic for Le Guide Gastronomique, Jean-Luc had demolished the reputations of Michelin-starred chefs with a single flick of his fountain pen. But tonight, he faced his most unforgiving reservation: Chez Penelope, a pop-up establishment operating out of a fluorescent-pink playhouse in his living room. The head chef, age three, slammed a hollow plastic skillet onto Jean-Luc’s lap and demanded sixty dollars in Monopoly cash before appetizers were even served.

The tasting menu began with an avant-garde deconstruction: a wooden velcro strawberry balanced precariously atop a slightly chewed green crayon, garnished with lint from beneath the couch. 'The chef shows startling audacity,' Jean-Luc whispered into his voice recorder, jotting notes as Penelope stared him down unblinkingly while drinking bath water from a teapot. 'The crayon brings a bold, waxy mineral acidity, though the mouthfeel suffers from severe textile contamination.'

For the entree, Penelope tossed a plastic hamburger bun across the carpet, declared it was 'chicken nuggets,' and immediately walked out of the kitchen to watch cartoons. Jean-Luc chewed thoughtfully on the empty air, brought to tears by the sheer, unbridled arrogance of the performance. His review ran on page one that Sunday: 'A searing indictment of modern fine dining. Service was feral and non-verbal; the chef abandoned her station mid-course. Four stars.'
